sources.title: Why Your Brain Hates Contradictions

excerpts.text: Instead of changing your understanding of the world, you found a way to preserve it.
The contradiction is carrying more than information. It is carrying consequences.
After all, a rationalisation rarely announces itself as one. It usually arrives dressed as an explanation.
Am I trying to understand what is true, or am I trying to preserve the person I believe myself to be?

sources.title: Cognitive Consequences of Forced Compliance
sources.publisher: Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58, 203–210

excerpts.text: Recently Festinger (1957) proposed a theory concerning cognitive dissonance
excerpts.locator: Introduction; reference: A Theory of Cognitive Dissonance, Row Peterson, 1957

excerpts.text: Seventy-one male students in the introductory psychology course at Stanford University ... His task was to turn each peg a quarter turn clockwise ... Three conditions were run, Control, One Dollar, and Twenty Dollars
in the Control condition the average rating was -.45 ... In the One Dollar condition ... the average rating was +1.35 ... The average rating in this condition [Twenty Dollar] is only -.05
excerpts.locator: Results, How Enjoyable the Tasks Were (Table 1); scale -5 to +5; 20 Ss per condition

excerpts.text: The greater the reward offered (beyond what was necessary to elicit the behavior) the smaller was the effect.

sources.reliability_notes: Classic peer-reviewed experiment; small samples (20 per condition) and a 1950s design; replications and reinterpretations exist.

sources.title: Do beliefs yield to evidence? Examining belief perseverance vs. change in response to congruent empirical findings

excerpts.text: Across four studies, participants consistently shifted their beliefs in response to the evidence, even when it challenged their views on religion (Studies 1–3), politics (Study 3), gun control (Study 3), and capital punishment (Studies 3–4). ... In some cases, bias emerged in participants' evaluations of evidence, but not in others.

sources.title: Neural basis of attitude change motivated by cognitive dissonance: a scoping review

excerpts.text: cognitive dissonance detection, with the anterior cingulate cortex playing a particularly relevant role, facilitates attitude change. Subsequently, the process of updating the representation of the stimulus value (attitude change) appears to be linked to the activity of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex

sources.reliability_notes: Scoping review of neuroimaging/stimulation studies; associations, not a single mechanism.

claims.text: Instead of changing your understanding of the world, you found a way to preserve it.
The contradiction is carrying more than information. It is carrying consequences.
A rationalisation rarely announces itself as one. It usually arrives dressed as an explanation.
Am I trying to understand what is true, or am I trying to preserve the person I believe myself to be?
Leon Festinger proposed the theory of cognitive dissonance in 1957.

In Festinger and Carlsmith's 1959 experiment, students did about an hour of boring tasks (including turning pegs), then some were paid $1 or $20 to tell the next participant the tasks were enjoyable; a control group was not asked.
Asked how enjoyable the tasks were (-5 to +5), the $1 group averaged +1.35, the $20 group -0.05 and the control group -0.45.
caveats: 20 participants per condition; a 1950s study with a small sample.

claims.text: A smaller external justification was associated with greater attitude change.

In four studies, people often shifted their beliefs in response to clear evidence, even on religion, politics and capital punishment; bias in evaluating evidence appeared in some cases but not others.
A 2026 scoping review linked detecting dissonance especially to the anterior cingulate cortex, and the later attitude updating to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
caveats: Associations across studies; brain regions do many jobs; no single 'contradiction detector'.
